sections.heading: Every Second Since 1970 Has a Number
paragraphs: APIs and databases track time as a single epoch number — seconds (or milliseconds) since January 1 1970 UTC. [timestamp-converter:Converting timestamps to dates] makes that integer mean something human again.

The Unix epoch is the universal backbone for event sequencing in software systems, from login tokens to analytics pipelines. When every millisecond matters, having a reliable converter between the numeric and human-readable forms eliminates guesswork entirely.
Both directions cover debugging and coding.

sections.heading: Seconds vs. Milliseconds
paragraphs: Platforms disagree: many APIs give seconds while JavaScript dates give milliseconds. The difference is three orders of magnitude, and mistaking one for the other produces dates decades in the past or far into the future.
The converter detects and supports both, labeled clearly so you always know which unit you are working with. A ten-digit number maps to seconds, a thirteen-digit number maps to milliseconds.
No more off-by-three-zeros confusion.
Understanding this distinction saves hours of debugging, especially when integrating data from multiple services that each pick a different convention.

sections.heading: Timezone Awareness Without Ambiguity
paragraphs: A timestamp is absolute in UTC; humans need their local view. Displaying both side by side prevents the all-too-common misinterpretation where an event appears to happen on the wrong day.
Local and UTC displays side by side eliminate misinterpretation. A team spread across New York, London and Tokyo can all reference the same epoch value while seeing it expressed in their own clocks.
Absolute truth, contextualized locally.
The converter also handles daylight saving transitions correctly, so timestamps that fall within a shift are shown with the appropriate offset rather than a misleading fixed offset.

sections.heading: Working with Negative Timestamps and Far-Future Dates
paragraphs: Not all timestamps sit comfortably in the 2000s and 2010s. Historical databases and legacy systems occasionally reference dates before 1970, producing negative epoch values that many tools refuse to display.

The converter handles negative inputs gracefully, showing dates before the Unix epoch without error. This is essential for scientific archives, retro computing projects and financial records that predate the epoch boundary.

On the opposite end, timestamps representing dates far into the future or far into the past test the limits of 32-bit integers. The converter works with full 64-bit precision, so values beyond the year 2038 and before 1901 render correctly.
These edge cases are rare in everyday work but critical when they appear.

sections.heading: Common Use Cases Across Industries
paragraphs: Software engineers convert timestamps daily when debugging API responses, validating JWT expiry claims or tracing event sequences through distributed systems. A single converted value often reveals the root cause of a time-sensitive bug.

Data analysts and scientists rely on epoch fields in datasets exported from ClickHouse, BigQuery or Elasticsearch. Converting these to readable dates makes exploratory analysis and visualization tools far more useful.

Security professionals inspect certificate validity periods, token lifetimes and audit logs where every entry is timestamped in epoch format. Accurate conversion ensures compliance checks and forensic investigations proceed on solid footing.
Even non-technical users occasionally encounter epoch values in spreadsheet exports from SaaS platforms, and a quick conversion removes the barrier between raw data and actionable information.
